questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of the cubic $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 - 15x + 4$.

options.why: Substituted the stationary values into $f'(x)$ instead of $f(x)$ to find the vertical coordinates.
Used the constant term $4$ as the vertical coordinate of both stationary points.
Reversed the signs of the roots of $f'(x) = 0$ before substituting into $f(x)$.

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is the cubic $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 24x + 11$ decreasing?

options.why: Found the intervals where the cubic is increasing instead of decreasing.
Swapped the signs of the roots of the quadratic derivative.
Omitted the lower turning point boundary when stating the interval.

questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary points of $f(x) = 6x^2 - 2x^3 + 5$.

options.why: Evaluated $f'(x)$ instead of $f(x)$ to find the vertical coordinates.
Added $2(2)^3$ instead of subtracting it when evaluating $f(2)$.

questions.question_text: Find the coordinates of the stationary point of $f(x) = (x + 2)^3 - 1$.

options.why: Evaluated $f'(-2)$ instead of $f(-2)$ to find the vertical coordinate.
Changed the constant term from $-1$ to $1$ when evaluating $f(-2)$.

questions.question_text: For what values of $x$ is $f(x) = x^3 + 2x^2 + 5x - 3$ increasing?

options.why: Used the vertex of the quadratic derivative as a boundary of increase without checking whether the derivative is positive on both sides.
Treated the interval where the derivative decreases as the interval where the original function increases.
Mistook the absence of real roots of $f'(x)$ for the absence of positive derivative values.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 3x^2 + 4x + 5$
$f'(x) = 3\left(x + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 + \dfrac{11}{3}$
Since $\left(x + \dfrac{2}{3}\right)^2 \geq 0$, $f'(x) \geq \dfrac{11}{3} > 0$.
Therefore $f(x)$ is increasing for all real $x$.

questions.question_text: For what values of $k$ does the cubic $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + kx + 8$ have no stationary points?

options.why: Divided $36 - 12k < 0$ by $-12$ without reversing the inequality sign.
Left the leading coefficient $a = 3$ out of $4ac$, using $\Delta = 36 - 4k < 0$.
Made both slips: used $\Delta = 36 - 4k$ without the $a = 3$, then failed to reverse the sign when dividing by $-4$.

questions.solution_text:
$f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x + k$
For no stationary points, $3x^2 - 6x + k = 0$ has no real solutions:
$\Delta = (-6)^2 - 4(3)(k) < 0$
$36 - 12k < 0$
$12k > 36$
$k > 3$
